title: The China AI Registry
abstract: A registry by Satoshi Yamauchi (Japanese title: 988の名簿) that transcribes every row of the attachments (delta lists) to the notices "Generative AI services filed (and registered)" published by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC). Providing a generative AI service in China requires filing (备案) with the authorities, and the CAC publishes the filed and registered services with company names roughly every two months. Rows are transcribed from the attachment PDFs in their source column positions and characters; typos, column shifts and carry-overs are not corrected but recorded as observation codes, and each attachment is identified by the SHA-256 of its PDF. Only rows printed in an attachment PDF are admitted; no row is created from press reports, provincial cyberspace offices or company announcements, and every row of a connected attachment is admitted without exception. Each serial-number series is kept as its own table: filings, on-device filings, anthropomorphic-interaction filings, registrations and filing changes. Filing changes are appended without rewriting the original filing row. Only the author writes to the registry, with PGP-signed commits. The canonical data is data/registry.json; one CSV per table and data/sources.csv are generated from it. The data specification (docs/DATA_SPEC.md) and the update runbook (docs/UPDATE_RUNBOOK.md) are published with the data. The repository also contains a structural analysis of China's AI industry that uses the registry as its population, in Japanese and English editions. This archived version (v1.3.1, 22 November 2026) joins Attachments 1 to 14 (April 2024 to October 2026): as of 31 October 2026, 1,234 filings, 10 on-device filings and 1 anthropomorphic-interaction filing (1,245 in total, matching the CAC cumulative figure), 955 registrations and 1 filing change. Its text and data are identical to v1.3; v1.3.1 adds only the citation files. title: Does Switching to Muon Hurt Fine-Tuning of Small Open Models? A Case Study on Qwen2.5-0.5B
abstract: Muon, an optimizer that orthogonalises the momentum update of each weight matrix, has become a strong alternative to AdamW for pretraining language models. Whether it should also be used to fine-tune the many open models pretrained with AdamW is less clear, and recent studies disagree: one reports a penalty for switching optimizers on a narrow task, another finds none in broad instruction tuning. Both rely mainly on models pretrained from scratch or on models of 4B parameters and above. I examine the question for a small, heavily trained open model, Qwen2.5-0.5B, fine-tuned with AdamW and with Muon on a narrow task (WikiText-2) and on broad instruction data (a Tulu-3 subset), with a separate learning-rate sweep for each optimizer and three seeds for every final configuration. Switching costs little on the target task: validation perplexity rises from 12.47 to 12.53 in the narrow setting, and the target loss does not get worse in the broad one. Forgetting, measured as the increase in loss on held-out web text, is almost entirely determined by how far fine-tuning moves the weights (r ≥ 0.998 across 38 runs), and at equal target loss Muon forgets 1.7–2.3 times more in the narrow setting. Muon saved 6% of peak GPU memory and ran 9–10% slower. At this scale I find little reason to switch.

title: The Co-Development of Artificial Cognitive Capabilities: An Integrative Theoretical Framework of Interdependent Reconfiguration, Epistemic Warrant, and Future Reachability
abstract: The development of artificial intelligence is commonly characterized in terms of computational efficiency, model scaling, learning performance, generalization, and the successful execution of increasingly complex tasks. However, the emergence of autonomous agents, self-revising scientific systems, and open-ended learning architectures raises a more fundamental question: under what conditions does an intelligent system acquire genuinely new cognitive capabilities, rather than merely improve the efficiency of capabilities it already possesses?This article develops an integrative theoretical framework for understanding the co-development of artificial cognitive capabilities through functionally interdependent transformations. Its central proposition is that cognitive development depends not only on the performance of individual mechanisms of representation, action, observation, validation, and metacognitive regulation, but also on the organization of dependencies among these mechanisms.Drawing upon information theory, statistical comparison of experiments, active perception, causal representation learning, epistemic iteration, metareasoning, and open-ended learning, the framework distinguishes informational accessibility, operational capability, epistemically warranted capability, and the future reachability of cognitive capabilities.Several conditional results are developed through explicit formal constructions. First, complementary improvements may jointly enable a cognitive capability that remains inaccessible under either improvement separately. Second, locally advantageous decision rules may fail to discover productive developmental trajectories when benefits depend on coordinated transformations. Third, the order of cognitive transformations may affect developmental outcomes when operations involve prerequisites, noncommutativity, irreversible costs, or resource limitations. Fourth, agents possessing equivalent current capabilities may nevertheless differ in the range of capabilities reachable through subsequent development.The article further distinguishes functional improvement, epistemic progress, and developmental progress, demonstrating why improvements in internal evaluation scores cannot automatically be interpreted as genuine advances in cognitive capability.The proposed framework does not claim the discovery of a new law of information theory or a universal mechanism governing all forms of intelligence. Its contribution is integrative and explanatory: it provides a unified conceptual and formal structure for investigating how interdependent cognitive processes can jointly alter the accessibility, justification, and future development of artificial cognitive capabilities.

title: LaSDAICVI: Children's Spanish Voice Commands Dataset
abstract: LaSDAICVI (LaSDAI Comandos de Voz Infantil) is a keyword-spotting dataset of Spanish speech recorded from 41 primary-school children aged 8 to 11 in Tucaní, Mérida state, Venezuela. It contains 29,061 isolated-word recordings (16 kHz, mono, 16-bit PCM WAV) of 60 keywords: the digits 0–9, the 32 results of the multiplication tables 2–9, and 18 voice commands. The release includes per-sample metadata (speaker ID, gender, age, grade), the official speaker-independent train/validation/test splits used in the thesis, background-noise clips for data augmentation, and the full B.Sc. thesis describing the recording protocol and baseline keyword-spotting models. Parents signed an informed consent form and each child signed an informed assent. The recordings are of minors: use them only for non-commercial research and education, do not attempt to identify participants, and do not use them for speaker identification, voice cloning or voice synthesis. Created at the Laboratorio de Sistemas Discretos, Automatización e Integración (LaSDAI), Universidad de los Andes, Mérida, Venezuela.

title: From Black-Box Computation to Causal Accessibility: Toward a Theory of Emergent Cognitive Capabilities in Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The increasing capabilities of artificial intelligence systems have intensified a fundamental question concerning the nature of machine intelligence: how can computational systems acquire cognitive capabilities that were neither explicitly programmed nor fully anticipated by their designers? Conventional explanations emphasize architectural complexity, parameter scaling, optimization, distributed representations, and the acquisition of increasingly sophisticated computational algorithms. Although these perspectives have substantially advanced the understanding of artificial intelligence, they do not completely resolve the distinction between information encoded within a system and information that can be functionally employed in generating intelligent behavior. This paper develops a theoretical framework centered on causal accessibility, defined as the context-dependent capacity of internally represented information to participate causally in task-relevant computational operations. The central hypothesis is that some changes in cognitive capability may arise not from the acquisition of fundamentally new representations or operations, but from changes in the functional accessibility, coordination, and compositional reuse of existing computational resources. The framework distinguishes representational availability, decodability, causal accessibility, compositional usability, and behavioral realization. It introduces a formal account of capability elicitation under fixed model parameters and specifies the conditions under which internal causal interventions could distinguish genuine functional access from mere informational correlation. Three theoretical propositions clarify why encoded information need not be behaviorally usable, why changes in accessibility can alter task performance without parameter modification, and why behavioral equivalence does not imply mechanistic equivalence. The proposed framework is situated in relation to mechanistic interpretability, causal abstraction, in-context learning, global workspace models, and theories of compositional intelligence. Its potential contribution is an integrated explanatory account of how latent computational resources may become operative cognitive capabilities. The paper does not claim to establish a novel fundamental law or provide new empirical findings. Instead, it offers a theoretically explicit and potentially falsifiable research program for investigating capability formation, emergence, and the organization of artificial intelligence.

title: When to Trust a Knowledge-Graph Walk: An Empirical Study of Per-Hop Decision Confidence
abstract: LLM-based question answering over knowledge graphs is accurate but expensive, and it rarely says when an answer is likely wrong. We study an old design, in which each hop of a walk is a classification over the current node's relations plus STOP, with a zero-shot, swappable decider, and ask what the walk's path confidence is worth on MetaQA, WebQSP, CWQ and a 2WikiMultiHopQA evidence graph. Where walks fail often enough to matter (MetaQA 3-hop, WebQSP), path confidence ranks right above wrong answers well (AUROC 0.82-0.97): the most confident half of MetaQA 3-hop answers is 99% accurate (81% overall). With the model and prompt fixed, reading token probabilities beats stated confidence by 0.09-0.23 AUROC and matches or beats 5-sample voting at a fifth of its cost. Raw confidence is overconfident, but a two-parameter Platt fit repairs much of that. The walk is less accurate than an LLM writing the relation path in one call, cheaper only on Freebase, and its confidence fails on CWQ. On 2Wiki, walks that never reached a decision were scored as certain; scoring them lowest lifts AUROC from 0.67 to 0.92, and to 0.85 on a held-out sample. As a strong agent's tool, the walk cuts cost by 17% at equal accuracy. The library, every run and the table scripts are released at https://github.com/manvirchakal/graphwalk.

title: Semantic Low-Code Data Fusion on the Edge to Support Intelligent Traffic Management
abstract: Intelligent traffic management applications require integrating data from diverse sources on the road infrastructure like radar sensors, cameras, and connected vehicles. The growing computational power deployed on the edge enables distributed computation of the data and near-real-time traffic control. However, interoperability is hindered by two key challenges: heterogeneous protocols for data access and inconsistent data semantics across sources. A data harmonisation solution is needed to retrieve data from different data sources while enabling a uniform representation of the information for data fusion and integrated analysis. The paper describes our solution to support the low-code definition of data integration pipelines by configuring a set of modular and reusable components. We leverage Semantic Web technologies and declarative mapping rules to resolve semantic inconsistency through a common conceptual model. A set of deployment templates enables the execution of the pipelines both on the cloud or on the edge to support diverse downstream applications with different performance and scalability requirements. Finally, the paper discusses the testing and validation of such a solution to support the reduction of collisions caused by unsafe braking at road intersections in a live deployment at the Mobility Lab in Helsinki.

Finally, the paper discusses the testing and validation of such a solution to support the reduction of collisions caused by unsafe braking at road intersections in a live deployment at the Mobility Lab in Helsinki.

title: Re-identification Risks and Privacy Challenges in Connected Vehicle Systems
abstract: CEDR’s Trusted Integrity and Authenticity for Road Applications (TIARA) project equips National Road Authorities with the tools and insights needed to develop secure and privacy-preserving data infrastructures for Cooperative Intelligent Transport Systems. In this paper we examine the privacy risks associated with C-ITS data, highlighting vulnerabilities in anonymisation methods and re-identification risks due to detailed data transmission, such as location and behavioural patterns. We explore state-of-the-art mitigation measures, including differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation, and federated learning. We also emphasize the importance of frameworks like pseudonymisation, data minimisation, and transparent data sharing. Our findings reveal significant privacy risks in C-ITS data, including vulnerabilities in anonymisation, re-identification threats through detailed data transmission, and the potential for behavioural profiling and location tracking. This emphasises the need for advanced mitigation measures, robust regulatory frameworks, and collaborative efforts among stakeholders to ensure secure and privacy-preserving use of connected vehicle data. Finally, we propose systemic and regulatory recommendation to road authorities, and provide a timeline from strategy to deployment based on short-, to mid- and long-term solutions.

title: Open, Distributed Research Ecosystems for Intelligent Transport Innovation in Europe
abstract: Modern transport systems increasingly rely on complex, heterogeneous datasets to inform research, planning, and policy. However, centralized approaches to data storage and analysis face significant challenges: they compromise data sovereignty, increase transfer costs, and often limit reproducibility due to privacy and ownership constraints. Recent advances in federated models offer a paradigm shift, allowing algorithms to travel to the data rather than the reverse. This approach supports privacy-preserving processing while aligning with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles of scientific data management. Within this architectural philosophy, the RAISE project has implemented a Mobility Pilot to explore the application of federated infrastructures in the transport domain. The pilot operates across three distributed computational nodes hosted by research institutions in Belgium, Spain, and Greece, applying federated analytic workflows to electric vehicle telemetry data. Analyses are executed locally on distributed nodes, validating a scalable, secure alternative to centralized analytics. Results demonstrate the feasibility of federated models in mobility research, offering insights into EV energy efficiency while ensuring reproducibility and data sovereignty. The study illustrates the potential of open, distributed research ecosystems to drive intelligent transport innovation across Europe.

title: Modal-Organizational Theory of Artificial Intelligence (MOTAI): Visual Atlas of Cognitive Organization, Capability Spaces, and Organizational Transformations
abstract: MOTAI Visual Atlas: Cognitive Organization, Capability Spaces, and Organizational Transformations This visual atlas provides a systematic graphical representation of the Modal-Organizational Theory of Artificial Intelligence (MOTAI), a conceptual and formal framework for investigating artificial intelligence through cognitive organization, functional capabilities, compositional structures, resource constraints, and organizational transformations. The atlas contains 17 pages of scientific diagrams, conceptual maps, comparative tables, and explanatory visualizations. It illustrates the central relationships between computational implementation, causal-functional organization, accessible cognitive operations, and the transformation of possibility spaces. Main components: The conceptual architecture and analytical levels of MOTAI. The formal organization of cognitive states, operators, admissible compositions, constraints, and resource costs. The distinction between actualized, operationally accessible, and transformationally accessible cognitive capabilities. Compositional closure and resource-bounded capability spaces. Four forms of cognitive and organizational transformation. Functional equivalence, capability comparison, and organizational incomparability. Seven formal properties and their conceptual implications. The relationship between structural organization, cognitive novelty, and changes in accessible capabilities. The visualizations are intended to support theoretical research in artificial intelligence, cognitive science, philosophy of computation, causal abstraction, and the study of complex intelligent systems. Scientific status: This atlas is a theoretical and conceptual resource. It does not present experimental findings or claim empirical validation. Its diagrams represent formal definitions, illustrative examples, and philosophical relationships rather than experimentally established neural mechanisms. Contents: A 17-page vector-based PDF visual atlas and a ZIP archive containing PNG versions of the atlas pages. Related research: The atlas accompanies the foundational MOTAI treatise and its independent formal model specification. Version: 1.0 (November 2026). Research framework: EMPIRAXIS Research.

title: The AI Forecast Registry
abstract: An append-only registry by Satoshi Yamauchi (Japanese title: 予測の名簿) of public forecasts about AI. Each row records the statement verbatim in its original language, with the sentence before and after, the date and the primary URL; describes the form of the forecast (the presence or absence of a deadline, a subject, a magnitude and a resolution condition) independently of whether it proves true; and fills the outcome only with what the forecaster later said about their own forecast and what a primary source states as fact. No verdict by the recorder appears. Registration and outcome are recorded as separate PGP-signed commits, so that a third party can verify that a forecast was registered before its outcome was known. Only the author writes to the registry; every forecast that meets the admission criteria is admitted, whether it warns of danger, argues for safety or denies that a capability is near. The registry begins on 22 March 2023 with the Future of Life Institute's open letter "Pause Giant AI Experiments." Rows are never rewritten: outcomes are appended to the canonical data as separate records. The canonical data is data/registry.json; data/registry.csv (rows as registered) and data/outcomes.csv (appended outcomes) are generated from it. Japanese and English editions. This archived version (v1.1, 22 November 2026) holds 23 rows (5 recorded after resolution, 18 before) and is the first version archived after an outcome was appended to a row registered before resolution: row 009, whose deadline was the week of 21 to 27 September 2026. The registry is updated roughly once a month, and a new version is archived in each month in which an outcome is appended. AIをめぐる公開の予測を記録する、山内怜史による追記専用の台帳。各行は、発言を原文の言語のまま直前・直後の一文とともに逐語で記録し、発言日と一次URLを付す。予測の形(期限・対象・尺度・決着条件の有無)は、予測が当たるかどうかとは独立に記述する。帰結には、予測者本人が後から自分の予測について述べた言葉と、一次資料に記載された事実だけを置き、記録者の判定は書かない。登録と帰結は別々の署名付きコミットで記録し、予測が帰結より前に登録されたことを第三者が検証できる。台帳に書くのは著者一人であり、収載基準を満たす予測は、危険を警告するものも、安全を主張するものも、能力の到来を否定するものも、同じ基準で載せる。起点は2023年3月22日のFuture of Life Institute公開書簡「Pause Giant AI Experiments」。行は書き換えず、帰結は正本に別の記録として追記する。正本は data/registry.json で、data/registry.csv(登録時の行)と data/outcomes.csv(帰結の追記)はそこから生成する。日本語版・英語版を収録。この版(v1.1、2026年11月22日)は23行(決着後に登録5行・決着前に登録18行)で、決着前に登録した行に帰結を追記した後の最初の保存版である(009、期限は2026年9月21日から27日の週)。台帳は月に1回程度更新し、帰結を追記した月ごとに新しい版を保存する。

title: Identity in the Age of AI: Toward a Functional Postphenomenology
abstract: Advanced AI systems increasingly mediate the cognitive and practical functions through which personal identity is enacted: intention formation, deliberation, memory, self-expression, preference formation, and relational interaction. Drawing on Western and Confucian conceptions of identity, this paper advances a functional hypothesis specifying six domains in which AI may be reorganizing the conditions of agency, and outlines the implications for responsibility, consent, dignity, and institutional design. The argument is functional and normative rather than metaphysical: not that agency disappears, but that the architecture of the self that is presupposed by our normative categories may require renewed examination.

title: Model choice and prompt framing in LLM sustainability judgments
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for sustainability assessment and decision support, yet their judgments may depend on the selected model and on how the task is defined. We compare 13 locally executed open-weight LLMs on 80 author-written sustainability scenarios using three prompt families that ask which actor should be responsible, bear the costs, or initiate action. Each model answered at two temperature settings with 100 repetitions, producing 624,000 deposited outputs, of which 610,708 contain a complete score vector. Scores were analyzed as relative actor support after removing each response’s overall level. Within this instrument, the cost prompt family produced the highest cross-model disagreement, exceeding both responsibility and catalyst by 7.37 points (question-cluster 95% intervals 5.56−9.15 and 5.38−9.36, describing variation across these 80 scenarios). It also produced the most lead-actor disagreement and the lowest full consensus. Moving from catalyst to cost reduced relative support for government and increased it for individuals and firms; moving from cost to responsibility largely reversed this pattern. These differences exceeded temperature-setting differences and persisted under model exclusion, alternative score transformations and tie rules, missing-response checks, and stems without explicit cost wording. Exploratory category patterns are conditional on uneven item coverage. Secondary rationale-language comparisons show the same within-model ordering but not the most cross-model variation under cost. Operational use should disclose model, prompt, and temperature choices; compare plausible alternatives; repeat generations; and refer high-disagreement judgments for human deliberation.

title: When Strong Reasoners Join the Pool: Small Union Premiums and Costly Runaway Generations in LLM Routing
abstract: Routing benchmarks often judge a router against a hindsight oracle that counts a query as solved whenever any model's recorded answer is correct, but under stochastic decoding that oracle mixes two different objects: the clairvoyant ceiling of committing to one model per query and the premium of calling several models and keeping any correct answer. A companion study measured this premium at 3.5 percentage points (pp) for 11 small open models on MATH-500; how large it is once current reasoning models enter the pool was unknown. We measure it with a fixed-protocol, pre-committed generation on a single NVIDIA B300: all 500 MATH-500 problems, 30 seeded samples per problem, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and NVIDIA's Nemotron Nano 9B v2 and Nemotron Super 49B v1.5 (a NAS derivative of the same 70B) under vendor sampling, a 65,536-token cap, a pinned Math-Verify scorer, and an append-only attempt ledger, for 45,000 scored responses. The two reasoning models both reach 96.1% accuracy against 76.2% for the 70B baseline. The empirical product-coupling premium is 0.215-0.588 pp across all two- and three-model pools; the empirical plug-in selection headroom over always calling Nano is 1.27 pp; and resampling Nano three times gives practically the same empirical any-correct rate as calling all three models once. Only 31 responses reached the cap, 25 of them with exactly periodic tails, yet the capped responses account for up to 60.2% of a model's output-length-squared proxy, and long generations made a fourth planned model, Llama-3.1-8B, too slow to finish. The premium is far below the companion's 3.5 pp, but models, pool size and protocol changed together; an oracle gap should therefore be reported with the pool, the protocol, the samples per cell and the decoding budget that produced it.

title: Mytho-MoE: Knowledge Graph Datasets, Model Checkpoints, and Experimental Evidence
abstract: This record contains research artifacts for Mytho-MoE, a question-level mixture of domain-specific LoRA experts using a frozen Qwen3-4B backbone. The system includes independently trained Harivamsha (HVM) and Ramayana (RaMO) expert adapters, an original mixed-task router, and a router further adapted using graph-derived natural-language questions. The release provides author-constructed RDF knowledge graphs, instruction datasets, router-adaptation splits, evaluation questions and reference answers, saved predictions, aggregate results, model checkpoints, and a snapshot of the accompanying code. Dataset construction used English translations of the Harivamsha Purana and the Ramayana of Valmiki available through Wisdom Library, with AI assistance and manual review. Source URLs and construction details are documented in the accompanying files. The expert instruction datasets contain 200,248 accepted training records and 22,100 validation records. Evaluation cohorts overlap and should not be treated as independent samples. An audit identified 588 HVM validation rows with identical task, query, and target records in HVM training. The release documents this overlap and other evaluation limitations. Handwritten diagnostic questions were used during development. See the README and verification reports for file descriptions, checkpoint requirements, reproduction instructions, and limitations.

title: Cross-MOBA player-behaviour reproducibility package (v1.1): companion code and data for "Modelling Human Player Behaviour with Attention-Based Artificial-Agent Networks: Cross-Context Transfer Learning between Dota 2 and Mobile Legends"
abstract: Companion code and data for the manuscript "Modelling Human Player Behaviour with Attention-Based Artificial-Agent Networks: Cross-Context Transfer Learning between Dota 2 and Mobile Legends" (manuscript CHBAH-D-26-00414, accepted in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans, Elsevier). title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B
abstract: Preservation mirror. This Zenodo record is a long-term preservation mirror of the official Hugging Face repository LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B published by LiquidAI, mirrored byte-for-byte at the pinned revision 3dc4cd09c9a2a99e1e819693e79d3aba5e9bb4f2 (revision tree). The deposit contains the complete 27-file repository snapshot (47,964,603,149 bytes) exactly as published upstream — no file was modified, converted, quantized or re-sharded. An identical preservation copy is held at the Internet Archive: archive.org/details/liquidai-lfm2-5-24b-a2b-hf-preservation-2026-001. License: LFM Open License v1.0 — https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B/blob/3dc4cd09c9a2a99e1e819693e79d3aba5e9bb4f2/LICENSE. The original license terms as published by LiquidAI govern; where the repository contains a LICENSE file it is included among the deposited files. The publisher's own model card (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B @ 3dc4cd09) follows, reproduced in full. Try LFM • Docs • Discord LFM2.5-24B-A2B LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with only 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B. Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19. Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap. Efficient inference: Runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. Find more information about LFM2.5-24B-A2B in our blog post. 🗒️ Model Details Model Parameters Description LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base 24B (2B active) Pre-trained base model for fine-tuning LFM2.5-24B-A2B 24B (2B active) Post-trained for agentic workloads LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a general-purpose text-only reasoning model with the following features: Total parameters: 24.0B Active parameters: 2.45B Number of layers: 40 (30 double-gated short convolution blocks + 10 GQA) Experts: 64 per MoE block, top-4 routing Training budget: 36 trillion tokens Vocabulary size: 128,000 Context length: 131,072 tokens Languages: English, Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Spanish, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, Hindi, Russian, Polish Generation parameters: temperature: 0.1 top_k: 50 repetition_penalty: 1.05 Model Description LFM2.5-24B-A2B Original model checkpoint in native format. Best for fine-tuning or inference with Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang. LFM2.5-24B-A2B-FP8 FP8 checkpoint (block-wise FP8 weights, dynamic FP8 activations). Best for high-throughput GPU serving with vLLM and SGLang with lower memory usage. LFM2.5-24B-A2B-GGUF Quantized format for llama.cpp and compatible tools. Optimized for CPU inference and local deployment with reduced memory usage. LFM2.5-24B-A2B-ONNX ONNX Runtime format for cross-platform deployment. Enables hardware-accelerated inference across diverse environments (cloud, edge, mobile). LFM2.5-24B-A2B-MLX-4bit MLX format for Apple Silicon. Optimized for fast inference on Mac devices using the MLX framework. LFM2.5-24B-A2B-DSpark DSpark draft model for speculative decoding with SGLang, for faster generation. Coming soon. We recommend using it for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. It is not recommended for knowledge-heavy tasks on its own: pair it with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength. Chat Template LFM2.5 uses a ChatML-like format. See the Chat Template documentation for details. Example: <|startoftext|><|im_start|>system You are a helpful assistant trained by Liquid AI.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user What is C. elegans?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant <think> You can use tokenizer.apply_chat_template() to format your messages automatically. [!TIP] 💡 Note: Unlike LFM2-24B-A2B, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a pure reasoning model that always thinks before it answers. It adds a <think> tag directly in the chat template when starting an assistant answer. Tool Use LFM2.5 supports function calling in four steps: Function definition: Provide the list of tools as a JSON object in the system prompt, or use tokenizer.apply_chat_template() with tools=.... Function call: By default, LFM2.5 writes Pythonic function calls (a Python list between <|tool_call_start|> and <|tool_call_end|> special tokens), as the assistant answer. You can override this behavior by asking the model to output JSON function calls in the system prompt. Function execution: Execute the call and return the result with the tool role. Final answer: LFM2.5 interprets the tool output and returns a plain-text answer addressing the original prompt. See the Tool Use documentation for the full guide. Example: <|startoftext|><|im_start|>system List of tools: [{"name": "get_candidate_status", "description": "Retrieves the current status of a candidate in the recruitment process", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"candidate_id": {"type": "string", "description": "Unique identifier for the candidate"}}, "required": ["candidate_id"]}}]<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user What is the current status of candidate ID 12345?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant <|tool_call_start|>[get_candidate_status(candidate_id="12345")]<|tool_call_end|>Checking the current status of candidate ID 12345.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>tool [{"candidate_id": "12345", "status": "Interview Scheduled", "position": "Clinical Research Associate", "date": "2023-11-20"}]<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant The candidate with ID 12345 is currently in the "Interview Scheduled" stage for the position of Clinical Research Associate, with an interview date set for 2023-11-20.<|im_end|> Training LFM2.5-24B-A2B keeps the LFM2-24B-A2B architecture with two changes: the context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and the vocabulary doubles from 65K to 128K tokens through an in-place tokenizer expansion for better non-Latin tokenization. Pre-training: ~33T tokens, up from ~17T. Mid-training: 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, then 300B tokens of long-context data at 131K context. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear in both phases. Post-training: supervised fine-tuning, teacher specialization, two multi-domain on-policy distillation stages (one non-agentic, one agentic), and agentic reinforcement learning inside popular agent harnesses (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, OpenCode), so the model learns their tools, system prompts, and interaction patterns. 🏃 Inference LFM2.5 is supported by many inference frameworks. See the Inference documentation for the full list. Name Description Docs Notebook Transformers Simple inference with direct access to model internals. Link vLLM High-throughput production deployments with GPU. Link SGLang High-throughput production deployments with GPU. Link — llama.cpp Cross-platform inference with CPU offloading. Link MLX Apple's machine learning framework optimized for Apple Silicon. Link — LM Studio Desktop application for running LLMs locally. Link — Quick start Get started with Transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0): from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextStreamer model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, device_map="auto", dtype="bfloat16", # attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" <- uncomment on compatible GPU ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) streamer = TextStreamer(tokenizer, skip_prompt=True, skip_special_tokens=True) prompt = "What is C. elegans?" input_ids = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt", tokenize=True, )["input_ids"].to(model.device) output = model.generate( input_ids, do_sample=True, temperature=0.1, top_k=50, repetition_penalty=1.05, max_new_tokens=4096, streamer=streamer, ) Agentic Harnesses LFM2.5-24B-A2B supports tool calling for agentic workflows. Serve it locally with any OpenAI-compatible backend from the table above, then configure your agent harness to connect to it. For full setup instructions including installation and additional options, see our Agent Harnesses guide. Hermes Either use the interactive wizard or set it directly: hermes config set model.provider custom hermes config set model.base_url http://localhost:8080/v1 hermes config set model.default LFM2.5-24B-A2B hermes config set model.context_length 131072 hermes config set model.api_mode chat_completions hermes config set agent.tool_use_enforcement true OpenClaw Add to your config in `models.providers`: local: { baseUrl: "http://localhost:8080/v1", apiKey: "sk-local", api: "openai-completions", models: [{ id: "LFM2.5-24B-A2B", name: "LFM2.5-24B-A2B", contextWindow: 131072, maxTokens: 8192, cost: { input: 0, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0 } }] } Pi Add to your config to `~/.pi/agent/models.json`: { "providers": { "local": { "baseUrl": "http://localhost:8080/v1", "api": "openai-completions", "apiKey": "local", "models": [{ "id": "LFM2.5-24B-A2B" }] } } } 🔧 Fine-Tuning We recommend fine-tuning LFM2.5 for your specific use case to achieve the best results. title: Federazione Semantica di Linked Open Data dell'Asia Orientale e Sud-Orientale, Ponti Cross-Dominio e Scoperta Automatica di Triadi Aperte Swanson ABC nell'Ipergrafo Rotta Aristeica Analisi Quantitativa di 11 Endpoint Live (#1240), 9 Vertici-Ponte Multi-Pilastro (#1242), Sensibilita' al Contesto Nullo Benjamini-Yekutieli e Demarcazione Fonologica (#1241- #1243)
abstract: La federazione di 11 infrastrutture Linked Open Data e Open Data dell'Asia Orientale e Sud-Orientale (5 nuovi endpoint W3C SPARQL 1.1 che portano la federazione da 24 a 29 nodi SPARQL attivi, affiancati da 6 distribuzioni RDF Turtle/JSON/XML API e dallo scarto documentato di 11 servizi non operativi) non genera di per sé alcuna scoperta automatica nel motore Swanson ABC fintanto che i nodi database e le sedi moderne restano isolati in quarantena (psca:swansonEligible=false) e i manufatti restano confinati a singoli articoli (78 triadi aperte complessive pre-ponti, 0 rigetti BY-FDR, score max 0.271811). Introducendo 9 vertici-ponte concettuali non geografici su 4 pilastri analitici (metallurgy_lia, linguistics_epigraphy, genetics_bio, material_cult_typology) e partizionando 4 iperarchi tematici di consenso (he728, he728_dongson_heger1, he728_kongorikishi_gandhara, he728_yayoi_bio_corridor) su 11.342 nodi @graph e 149.561 triple RDF SHACL-conformi, il numero di triadi aperte sale a 185 (Top-10 mediana +0.3295 vs baseline mono-dominio, MW p = 1.827e-04, Hedges g = 10.50). Dopo calibrazione su permutazioni, coda continua di Knijnenburg GPD e correzione conservativa Benjamini-Yekutieli (α = 0.05), emerge 1 associazione statisticamente significativa (Chang'an Q6501000 ↔ Linzi CHGIS hvd_85232, score = 0.73331, q_BY = 9.343e-05), mentre Cheonmachong (Gyeongju) ↔ Chang'an evidenzia un'istruttiva sensibilità al contesto nullo (q_BY = 0.01463 pre-#1243 vs 0.05921 post-#1243) e le piste Dian-Dong Son e Daisenryo Kofun rimangono ipotesi esplorative non significative a q_BY > 0.58. Parallelamente, gli audit #1241 e #1243 falsificano le convergenze grafiche tra Yaz (Tifinagh /z/), il carattere 木 (*C.mˤok > mù) su shuowen.space, 朱/銖 (*tjo/*djo > zhū [ʈʂu]) e i papiri di Cnosso. title: Privacidad y seguridad en sistemas de aprendizaje federado: revisión de métodos y desafíos computacionales
abstract: Federated learning enables model training on distributed information without necessarily centralizing raw records. Nevertheless, parameter exchanges, participant coordination, and malicious behavior create threats that do not disappear when data remain at their source. This paper examines privacy and security safeguards in federated learning systems and their computational trade-offs. A structured narrative literature review was conducted through a targeted search of verifiable academic sources and thematic analysis of foundational studies, methodological contributions, and surveys. Findings distinguish inference and reconstruction attacks, model poisoning, backdoors, and server-related threats, and compare differential privacy, secure aggregation, robust optimization, and verification mechanisms. The reviewed literature suggests that no single method simultaneously guarantees confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Appropriate protection depends on the threat model, architecture, accuracy requirements, communication overhead, and computational constraints. Trustworthy deployment, therefore, requires complementary safeguards, explicit evaluation metrics, and reproducible tests tailored to each use case.

title: imr-anomaly-validation-ru: data and code for validating anomaly-detection algorithms on Russian regional infant mortality data, 2015–2023
abstract: Data and code for: Rusova V. S. Error Detection in Russian Infant Mortality Data: Validating Anomaly Detection Algorithms. Vestnik MIRBIS (version 2.0 of the article published as Vestnik MIRBIS, 2026, 1(45): 182–192, DOI 10.25634/MIRBIS.2026.1.20). The repository contains the regional panel of live births, infant deaths and the published infant mortality rate for 85 constituent entities of the Russian Federation, 2015–2023, reconciled cell by cell with the Rosstat operational bulletins included in data/raw; the computational scripts of all stages of the analytical protocol; machine-readable results of each stage, figures and execution logs; unit tests of the statistical methods; documentation of every analytical decision and a table linking each quantity reported in the article to the file in which it is computed. The analysis tests an anomaly-detection algorithm at three levels: its own computations, its operating characteristics on synthetic data with known anomalies and under admissible analytical specifications, and the limits of what is observable from aggregated data. A flag is a reason to check primary records, not evidence of an error; the absence of flags is not evidence that the data are free of distortion. Reproduce: pip install -r requirements.txt; python run_all.py (about one minute). Random numbers come from named streams derived from one seed (20260123), so runs are bit-for-bit repeatable. Licences: code under MIT (LICENSE); derived data, results and documentation under CC BY 4.0 (LICENSE-DATA). Files in data/raw are official Rosstat publications reproduced unchanged.

title: Dual-Role Evaluation of Large Language Models in Cybersecurity: A Unified Framework for Offensive Generation and Defensive Intelligence
abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) is reshaping cybersecurity by strengthening defensive capabilities while simultaneously enabling increasingly sophisticated offensive threats. Despite this dual-use nature, existing evaluation methodologies remain fragmented and commonly assess LLMs in isolation as either offensive or defensive systems. This work presents a unified dual-role evaluation framework that characterizes LLM behavior within a shared cybersecurity context through a multi-dimensional taxonomy encompassing role, capability, intent, and contextual use. The framework is empirically evaluated under a strictly single-turn setting (T = 1), in which each offensive input is independently assessed through one corresponding defensive response. The evaluation covers phishing detection, prompt injection, log analysis, malware reasoning, vulnerability exploitation, and incident response using malicious, benign, and ambiguous scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate strong overall detection performance, low error rates, and effective handling of dual-use and borderline cases through ambiguity-aware classification. The findings further reveal the difficulty of distinguishing malicious intent from structurally similar benign inputs, underscoring the importance of context-sensitive evaluation and uncertainty-aware decision making in cybersecurity applications. Overall, the study establishes a controlled and reproducible single-turn baseline for evaluating offensive inputs and defensive LLM responses across diverse cybersecurity tasks.

title: Métodos de inteligencia artificial explicable: revisión de técnicas, aplicaciones y limitaciones
abstract: La inteligencia artificial explicable (XAI) agrupa procedimientos orientados a facilitar el examen de predicciones, representaciones y comportamientos de sistemas de aprendizaje automático. Este artículo analiza las principales familias de técnicas, sus ámbitos de aplicación y sus limitaciones, mediante una revisión narrativa estructurada de publicaciones académicas verificables. Se incorporan elementos de búsqueda y organización documental empleados en estudios bibliométricos, pero no estima indicadores de producción científica ni declara exhaustividad. Se clasifican las propuestas en modelos intrínsecamente interpretables, explicadores locales aproximados, atribuciones basadas en contribuciones, métodos de gradientes, explicaciones contrafactuales y enfoques globales. Los resultados muestran que cada familia responde a una pregunta explicativa distinta y exige criterios particulares de evaluación. LIME aproxima decisiones individuales, SHAP distribuye atribuciones entre variables bajo supuestos definidos, los gradientes caracterizan sensibilidades en redes diferenciables y los contrafactuales identifican modificaciones capaces de alterar resultados. La utilidad de estos recursos se encuentra limitada por inestabilidad, dependencia de distribuciones de referencia, problemas de fidelidad, restricciones causales y divergencias entre evaluación técnica y comprensión humana. Se concluye que una explicación no debe equipararse con validación, causalidad, equidad o confiabilidad del modelo.

Los resultados muestran que cada familia responde a una pregunta explicativa distinta y exige criterios particulares de evaluación. LIME aproxima decisiones individuales, SHAP distribuye atribuciones entre variables bajo supuestos definidos, los gradientes caracterizan sensibilidades en redes diferenciables y los contrafactuales identifican modificaciones capaces de alterar resultados. La utilidad de estos recursos se encuentra limitada por inestabilidad, dependencia de distribuciones de referencia, problemas de fidelidad, restricciones causales y divergencias entre evaluación técnica y comprensión humana. Se concluye que una explicación no debe equipararse con validación, causalidad, equidad o confiabilidad del modelo.

title: A Near Neighbour Is Not a Native Feature: What Nearest-Neighbour Novelty Detection Owes to the Space It Measures In, Why the Case For and Against Pretrained Features Turns on Benchmark and Baseline More Than on Where the Features Came From, and the Comparison That Would Separate Scoring Rule From Representation
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research A novelty detector is trained on normal data and asked to flag whatever is unlike it. Since 2020 two positions have competed over how such a detector should be built. One holds that the decisive ingredient is a feature space borrowed from a network pretrained on a large external corpus, after which a nearest-neighbour distance is enough, and that self-supervised or reconstruction-based detectors trained only on the normal data are outclassed. The other holds that detectors trained in-domain, such as autoencoders whose novelty score combines the reconstructions of an input's nearest latent neighbours with the distance to them, are competitive without any pretrained network and transfer to domains, such as radio-telescope spectrograms, that look nothing like natural photographs. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two positions are answering a question neither benchmark design isolates. A published comparison of two detectors almost always changes at least three things at once: the space in which distance is measured, the rule that turns distance into a score, and the kind of novelty the benchmark plants, while a fourth factor, the evaluation (metric, baseline implementation, hyperparameter selection), decides which of the three gets the credit. On one industrial benchmark, published image-level results for detectors that all use ImageNet features and a distance or density score range from 75.0 to 99.1 AUROC, a spread several times larger than the 3.3-point margin by which the nearest-latent-neighbour autoencoder beats its own re-implementation of the pretrained baseline. On one natural-image benchmark, supervised ImageNet features with a simple density score are reported at 80.0, 86.2 and 92.5 AUROC by three groups. Off the pretraining distribution the verdict flips with the dataset: in one seven-dataset medical study a plain autoencoder beats frozen ImageNet features on two datasets and loses by up to 36 points elsewhere, and an autoencoder whose residual is measured in pretrained feature space beats both on most. The paper consolidates nineteen published results in a table and a figure, states a procedure for crediting a novelty-detection gain to a representation's origin rather than to the scoring rule or the evaluation, and names the studies that would settle what remains open.

title: LLM 的甜区:可定义、可表述、有数据、可验证的问题(数字生命·讨论稿)
abstract: 讨论稿。提出一个判断框架:LLM 的"甜区" = 同时满足四个条件的问题:①存在确切的函数;②现有数学工具能准确表述它;③现实中或模拟中存在大量数据;④结果可验证(或有可靠检查器)。四条件齐备时逼近器发挥最大作用;缺一个就要用别的手段补(形式化、模拟器、实验、人工验证),能力打折。给出边界情形(半甜区:数据少/验证弱/表述难/无函数)与例子表(数学、代码、棋、肥皂泡/极小曲面、天气、开放写作、价值判断、罕见天文事件逐条对照四条件)。与能力极限的关系:甜区不是没有极限,而是"四道门里最宽的地"(熵/预算/验证/可计算性仍生效)。给出工程判据:拿到新任务按四问检查(可定义?可表述?有数据?可验证?),任一不能就找替代路径。边界:定性框架、无量化阈值、未做系统实验检验;条件间不独立;可能存在反例;与已有讨论(压缩即智能、验证器引导、缩放律)有重叠但未做文献对照。

title: Monte Carlo Simulation of 2D Bearing-Only Object Localization Using Weighted and Unweighted Nonlinear Least Squares
abstract: Python software implementing a Monte Carlo simulation framework for two-dimensional bearing-only object localization. It compares weighted and unweighted nonlinear least-squares estimators for three- and four-station observation configurations and reports accuracy and covariance-based uncertainty metrics.

title: LingSante-Pulse: Unified Physiological Pretraining through Random-Feature Prediction and Cross-Modal Alignment
abstract: Clinical monitoring and wearable devices capture complementary physiological signals, but their partially overlapping modality coverage makes within-signal information and cross-modal relationships difficult to exploit jointly. We introduce LingSante-Pulse, a unified, general-purpose and flexible physiological representation framework that learns from these heterogeneous recordings. A shared, signal-conditioned encoder processes each physical channel independently and supports different numbers and combinations of signals for multimodal assessment and single-sensor inference. Pairwise cross-modal alignment, structured random-feature prediction (RFP) and masked waveform reconstruction jointly learn physiological relationships and preserve informative within-signal structure. Across 38 general physiological task configurations spanning PPG, ECG, EEG and EMG, the frozen encoder achieves the best dataset-balanced mean rank in each domain. In sleep assessment, multimodal staging on the HMC dataset and EEG-only staging on the Sleep-EDF dataset reach Macro-F1 scores of 0.7784 and 0.7941, respectively, while single-lead ECG apnea screening achieves an AUROC of 0.9183. Controlled experiments show that function prediction and waveform reconstruction provide complementary supervision for retaining temporal and rhythmic information. Representations learned under continually refreshed random supervision generalize to unseen teacher realizations, and correct auxiliary modality correspondence improves respiration-only representations. These results demonstrate that a single encoder can learn reusable physiological features across signal types, prediction targets and sensor configurations from partially overlapping recordings.

title: Improved Accuracy Scaling with Problem Complexity in LLM Arithmetic Reasoning Using Executable Symbolic Representations
abstract: High accuracy on mathematical benchmarks does not establish whether reasoning remains reliable as problem complexity increases. We examine how executable symbolic representations change accuracy scaling in large language models compared with natural-language reasoning. To address this limitation, we introduce the GSM Arithmetic Benchmark (GSM-AB), a controlled benchmark that independently varies operand digit length and operation count to probe numerical scale and compositional complexity. We find that executable representations can improve accuracy and slow its decline as complexity increases. Lean reduces average sensitivity to operand digit length at every tested model size. By contrast, slower degradation with increasing operation count emerges at the larger model sizes. A Python program-of-thought (Python-PoT) control shows a similar operation-axis pattern, suggesting that this finding is not specific to Lean. These findings show that reasoning representation shapes arithmetic accuracy scaling and support executable symbolic representations for more reliable reasoning on complex arithmetic tasks.

title: Backbone-Specific LoRA Geometry: Orthogonality, Superposition, and Provenance
abstract: Sharing one low-rank adaptation (LoRA) update across pretrained models simplifies deployment. Composition methods typically combine updates from a common backbone, while cross-model transfer transforms updates for a target backbone. The conditions for sharing updates across backbones while preserving accuracy and distinguishing individual contributions remain unclear. Our idea is to use backbone-specific update directions as signatures of their training backbones. We derive a cross-backbone correlation bound from attention symmetries and equivariant LoRA learning under independent, uniform pretrained feature orientations. A local gradient-flow model explains positive mean correlation between independent runs on the same backbone and task. These patterns motivate cosine-based backbone identification and inner-product tests for registered-adapter reuse without coordinate alignment. Experiments on CLIP backbones show that shared sums achieve nearly the same mean accuracy as separate adapters. Cosine scores reliably identify source backbones across the evaluated tasks. Registered adapters remain detectable in sums of adapters from different backbones.

title: DepthMSA: Combinatorial Training and Budget-Aware Depth Allocation for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
abstract: State-of-the-art multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) models rely on large pretrained encoders, yet typically process every modality to its full depth, regardless of its computational cost or predictive contribution. This raises a fundamental question: how should limited computation be allocated across modalities to preserve predictive performance? We reveal a substantial mismatch between the computational cost of modality encoders and the predictive benefit of processing them more deeply, suggesting that different modalities require different encoding depths. However, enabling heterogeneous depths introduces a key challenge: representations extracted at different depths must still be effectively fused. To address this, we propose $\textbf{DepthMSA}$, a budget-aware framework that supports flexible modality depths within a single MSA model. Specifically, we introduce combinatorial anytime training, which supervises the fusion head across all cross-modal depth combinations using a single full-depth encoder pass. At inference, a training-free, cost-aware allocator selects the configuration with the lowest validation-calibrated error under a sample-specific FLOPs budget. On CMU-MOSEI, DepthMSA maintains accuracy within one percentage point of the full-depth model while reducing measured FLOPs by 45\%, or by 82\% with a separately trained skip-enabled variant. When a CLIP visual encoder dominates computation, the allocation shifts toward reducing visual depth, achieving 56\% fewer FLOPs at unchanged accuracy. Compared with ADMN, an adaptive layer-allocation method that trains a controller for each budget, the skip-enabled variant reaches its accuracy with 3.2$\times$ fewer FLOPs and lower latency, without any per-budget training. Our project is available at https://pwang322.github.io/DepthMSA/.

title: EDAGoat: An EDA-Aware Agent for Project-Level GPU Optimization
abstract: GPU acceleration has transformed electronic design automation (EDA), yet further improving expert-engineered GPU tools still demands substantial manual effort. Automating this work calls for coding agents that can trace bottlenecks across host and device code while preserving correctness and design quality. We introduce EDAGoat, to our knowledge the first EDA-aware GPU optimization agent for this task. Its optimization enhancement (OE) mode guides edits with four cross-project GPU optimization patterns. Its mandatory validation (MV) mode requires the agent to test the edited program against the EDA constraints its changes could affect. Our benchmark covers five GPU EDA projects across four task families and 55 circuit inputs, measuring complete-solve runtime and verifying the resulting designs. Each configuration runs three independent searches per project. A search qualifies only if its solver passes correctness and design-quality checks on all public and hidden inputs. With DeepSeek, generic prompting qualifies in 7 of 15 searches and OE in 6 of 15, despite a higher best speedup on four projects. Adding MV raises this to 13 of 15 and, on every project, exceeds both generic baselines in mean and best speedup and OE in mean speedup; the geometric mean of per-project mean speedups rises from 1.11x (1.36x with OE) to 1.53x. With GPT-6 Astra, EDAGoat qualifies in all 15 searches and improves both speedup metrics over generic prompting on every project, lifting the same geometric mean from 1.26x to 1.57x. These results show that agents can use EDA knowledge to find further speedups in expert-tuned tools while preserving design correctness and quality, establishing EDA-aware GPU optimization as a new direction for agent research.

title: cmHC: Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction
abstract: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extends residual connections to multiple streams and stabilizes residual propagation by constraining stream-mixing residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. In this work, we investigate how to effectively mix residual streams within the Birkhoff polytope. We reveal a mixing trade-off: when under-mixed residual matrices stay close to the vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, hyper-connections will degenerate into a set of nearly independent streams; when over-mixed residual matrices are concentrated around the uniform barycenter of the polytope, streams will become less distinguishable from each other. We theoretically validate our findings by bounding the cumulative residual mixing, stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients across layers. Motivated by these findings, we propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), an exact doubly stochastic method which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior. This contraction mitigates under-mixing by forcing the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope, with a provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization. Moreover, we apply a moderate contraction at the shallow layers to prevent over-mixing, enabling stable gradient propagation on extremely large-scale model pretraining. Extensive experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models at various parameter scales demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. We also develop fused operators for cmHC on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%.

title: How Much of a Calculation-Error Rate Is Not Arithmetic: Auditing the FinReason Cup 2026 Task 3 Metric with a Deterministic Rule System
abstract: Task 3 of the FinReason Cup 2026 scores a system on two values per case, the one an XBRL filing reports and the one its own calculation relationships imply, and labels each failure as structural, extraction or calculation. This report shows that the calculation-error rate so defined does not count arithmetic failures, and bounds how far it is from one using the published board alone. One of the three rules behind the benchmark, DQC_US_0015, has an answer that is the negation of the reported value (in all 110 published practice cases, against 1 of 120 and 6 of 102 for the other two), so a calculation label on such a case records a wrong fact or a wrong route, not a wrong sum. Subtracting the available structural and extraction labels from each entry's error count on that rule gives a floor: the bound is positive for 22 of the 23 ranked entries, and at the top it is sharpest, with at least 11 of 12 and 12 of 13 calculation errors of the two joint-first entries falling on cases where no arithmetic remained. The calculation-error rate of the best systems on this task is almost entirely not arithmetic. The vehicle for that result is an entry that reconstructs the three data-quality rules the benchmark is drawn from, DQC_US_0015, DQC_US_0117 and DQC_US_0126, as a deterministic system with no learned parameters, no training step and no external service, running all 680 cases in 1.4 seconds. It scores 96.62% under the offline judge on development and 95.29% on the published test set, and its residual error concentrates in cases where a concept carries several equally flagged facts and the question names no dimensional member. Reading those error classes against the per-rule accuracies is what exposed the metric, which is why both are reported here.

abstract: 数字化转型加速了人工智能对社会生活的影响，传统伦理体系遭遇前所未有的挑战，而佛教拥有的智慧及严格的戒律要求，因果的法则，将成为人工智能的伦理治理提供有效的参考。本文先厘清人工智能发展现状及问题，然后系统讨论数字化场景中佛教修行及传播所面临的新问题，由此引出研究目标及核心问题：AI伦理可借鉴佛教“缘起性空”思想，促进人机良性互动，避免技术滥用。但佛教伦理在数字化转型中也面临信仰形式异化、传统遭解构、伦理落地难等问题。本文提出融合佛教智慧构建多元共治的AI伦理体系、推动佛教自身数字化良性转型、搭建人机共生的伦理体系等路径，让技术发展与人文伦理彼此协调、互为促进，最终实现“科技为体，佛法为魂”的良性互动。

title: Lift Out, Kick In: Decoupling Event Effects for Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Real-world time series are often shaped by exogenous events whose effects are superimposed on the system's underlying temporal dynamics. Historical observations therefore entangle persistent dynamics with event-induced deviations, making it difficult to determine which patterns should be extrapolated and which should be attributed to specific event contexts. Existing event-aware forecasting methods can incorporate event information or model event-related variation, but typically treat historical event attribution and future event generation separately. We propose Loki (Lift Out, Kick In), a general event-aware forecasting framework built on a shared Event Response Function (ERF). The ERF models event effects according to event type and relative temporal position and is shared across the historical and forecast windows. Loki lifts out estimated event-induced deviations from historical observations before forecasting, then uses the same ERF to kick in responses to known future events. This formulation separates event-response modeling from temporal forecasting while coupling historical attribution and future generation through a shared mechanism. Across five forecasting benchmarks, Loki achieves the best standardized MAE on all five datasets, reducing error by approximately 2.2%-11.7% over the strongest non-Loki baseline. Ablations and controlled analyses further support the roles of Lift Out, Kick In, shared response modeling, and compatibility across forecasting backbones.

title: 短视频中生成式人工智能的法律风险与规制
abstract: 随着短视频平台兴起与生成式人工智能技术的发展，生成式人工智能技术与短视频内容的生产与传播深度融合，在激发创作者创作动力的同时，也催生著作权侵权、人格权侵害以及数据安全泄露等多种法律风险。这类风险的传播路径有别于一般网络侵权，现行以避风港原则为核心的平台责任框架已经难以应对。本文通过对三类典型风险进行系统性梳理，进而从规范体系、侵权责任主体以及因果关系认定三个角度分析我国短视频中生成式人工智能的规制困境。在此基础之上，提出制度方案以实现权益保护与技术促进的动态平衡。

title: A Frugal AI Framework for India: Responsible and Right-sized AI
abstract: India's AI debate often swings between two insufficient options: replicating the compute-intensive, capital-heavy foundation-model programmes of the United States or China, or remaining a downstream adopter of foreign AI with localised interfaces and safeguards. Neither serves a country that must deliver AI to a very large, diverse population across uneven infrastructure and within constrained budgets. This white paper from the Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), IIT Madras, proposes a third path: Responsible Frugal AI, which applies principle-based frugal engineering alongside Responsible AI. Responsible Frugal AI is right-sized AI: it fixes the functional requirement first, asks whether AI is needed at all, and then chooses the smallest sufficient model, meeting the requirement with minimal resources while keeping a verified margin, robustness and responsible governance. The framework applies frugality across four dimensions (data, compute, model and operations) through seven levers spanning the AI lifecycle, each with practices and measures. It calls for public AI rails, vernacular-first design, measured resource use, human oversight for high-stakes decisions, and a cap on total resource consumption so that efficiency gains are not cancelled out by rising usage. We argue that India is resource-imbalanced rather than resource-poor, and that frugal principles offer the most viable route to population-scale deployment, fit naturally with India's digital public infrastructure, and make sovereignty operational by preserving India's capacity to specify, deploy, govern, inspect and adapt its AI systems. A seven-point adoption checklist and eleven policy statements translate the framework into practice, positioning AI in India as a responsible, frugal public-value system that maximises social value per rupee and per joule.

title: SCAP: Stochastic Context for Action Expert Pretraining
abstract: Single-modality action-expert pretraining controls competition from visual shortcuts before vision--language--action (VLA) adaptation. Yet single-modality pretraining can impair the vision--language interactions needed for subsequent joint prediction. We construct a diagnostic model in which VA or LA pretraining can disable an initially active pathway for joint vision--language modeling. In this model, subsequent training with complete visual and language inputs cannot restore the pathway, even with unlimited adaptation. We therefore introduce Stochastic Context for Action Expert Pretraining (SCAP), a new action-expert pretraining stage that precedes full-input training. During this stage, visual and text tokens are randomly masked before entering the VLM. In this unified diagnostic model, SCAP can preserve the joint vision--language modeling pathway during pretraining and subsequent full-input training. Compared with direct full-input training, it can also reduce reliance on visual shortcuts and increase reliance on language instructions. SCAP consistently improves performance across four different VLA architectures. In real-robot experiments, it achieves 76.67% average success across three instruction-conditioned manipulation tasks, outperforming full-input pretraining by 25 percentage points.

title: What Does Matching a Human Intervention Effect Establish? Benchmark Checks for LLM Simulations
abstract: LLM simulations are validated by equivalence with human effects, yet a zero reference passes whenever the human 90 percent interval lies inside the margin, as the human benchmark shows before simulation. When the zero reference fails, planned precision gives independent simulations the margin up to which passing is a 5 percent test of response. In an exploratory 70-experiment reanalysis, 72 percent of GPT-4's $\pm$0.20 SD passes were zero-reference passes; GPT-4 passed 16 contrasts the zero reference failed (1.58 expected without response). In a preregistered audit, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed three intention targets, all zero-reference passes, and the registered belief-gradient control; norm beliefs changed 0.065 SD against humans' 0.351 (zero-reference check added after unblinding; norm beliefs emphasized after inspection). Registered tests detected no overestimation; average-effect intervals excluded overestimation above 0.08 SD. A group audit's precision floor is 1.33 facts against a 2.9-fact effect. Report the zero-reference threshold beside every equivalence decision.

title: GEG-SAM: Gaze Exploration-Guided Segment Anything Model for Weakly Supervised Polyp Segmentation
abstract: Endoscopist gaze offers an unobtrusively acquired record of lesion-oriented visual exploration during routine clinical inspection, providing relevant supervision for tasks. However, existing methods treat fixations as isolated spatial prompts directly associated with the target, overlooking the fact that natural gaze records a continuous visual search process in which fixations are temporally connected, spatially organized, and coupled with the visual content. Interpreting each fixation independently based only on its local visual content overlooks the temporal evolution and spatial organization of the gaze trajectory, whereas modeling relations among fixations alone cannot reveal the visual semantics of the regions they attend to. To this end, we propose the Gaze Exploration-Guided Segment Anything Model (GEG-SAM), a principled weakly supervised framework designed to explicitly exploit structured gaze relations and their corresponding visual cues to modulate SAM for polyp segmentation. Specifically, GEG-SAM captures structured gaze relations by modeling the temporal dynamics and spatial topology of gaze exploration. It then associates these relational representations with fixation-aligned visual context to derive gaze-conditioned tokens, which are further injected into the frozen SAM encoder to modulate its pretrained image features. In this way, GEG-SAM effectively exploits the rich information embedded in gaze exploration to guide SAM toward lesion-oriented segmentation. Extensive experiments on five public polyp segmentation datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, improving the mean Dice by 9.30 percentage points over the strongest weakly supervised baseline.

title: Tripwire: Robot Agents that Program Their Own Interrupts under Human Disturbance
abstract: Agent harnesses are turn-based: the agent acts, waits for the result, then reasons. When the action invokes a pretrained robot policy, such as a vision-language-action (VLA) or world action model (WAM), the policy may react continuously to observations, but the agent cannot revisit its decision until the call returns. Meanwhile, a person may step into the robot's path or move the object it is about to grasp. Invoking the agent more often narrows this blind interval, but a reasoning model takes seconds per decision and most control steps need no new one. We propose TRIP, a training-free, event-driven harness in which the agent programs its own interrupts. With each call, the agent writes a tripwire: a lightweight, stateful Python program that runs alongside the policy, can query a compact VLM (for example, to locate a person and measure their distance), and decides whether the call continues or control returns to the agent. When it fires, the harness halts the policy and returns control with the reason; the agent then reassesses, adapts, and continues under a rewritten tripwire. We evaluate TRIP with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD, a benchmark of 168 RoboCasa365 scenes in which a simulated person disturbs the robot and any human-robot contact counts as failure. Compared with a turn-based harness using the same agent and tools, TRIP halves the rate of human contact with the strongest policy, raising safety from 61.3% to 81.3%, without sacrificing task success (38.7% vs. 31.0%). Real-robot experiments show that TRIP completes two manipulation tasks under human interference where the turn-based harness and the policy alone largely fail.

title: The Dogma of the Legal Unprotectability of Style
abstract: This research critically challenges the traditional dogma that styles are not eligible for legal protection against the backdrop of the GenAI revolution. AI tools enable anyone to generate new images, musical works and texts in the style of their favourite artists within seconds and at little or no cost. This raises the question of the extent to which styles may qualify for legal protection and whether such protection is desirable in the first place. Remarkably, legal scholarship that firmly maintains that styles are not eligible for legal protection has failed to clearly define what should be understood by ‘style’. Accordingly, this study first examines the meaning of ‘style’. In the absence of a legal definition, an interdisciplinary approach was adopted. The meaning of ‘style’ was explored across the disciplines from which legal scholarship has drawn the concept: linguistics, music and the visual arts. For the purposes of this study, ‘style’ is understood exclusively as a set of formal characteristics that recur consistently within a particular group of creations. Where these creations can be attributed to a single creator, the term ‘personal style’ is used. Where, by contrast, the creations originate from different creators but are related on some other basis, the term ‘general style’ is used. Examples include the style of a particular period, school, region or culture. Through a comparative legal study of the Netherlands, the United States and the United Kingdom, this research examines the protection of personal and general styles under copyright law, design law and unfair competition law.

title: HumanoidPose: Monocular 3D Pose Estimation for Humanoid Robots
abstract: As humanoid robots increasingly enter real-world environments, recovering their 3D whole-body pose from monocular imagery is becoming increasingly important for external state perception, motion analysis, and robot learning. However, Humanoid Robot Pose Estimation (HRPE) lies at the intersection of conventional Robot Pose Estimation (RPE) and Human Pose Estimation (HPE), while not being fully addressed by either paradigm: RPE primarily focuses on non-humanoid robots, particularly fixed-base manipulators, whereas HPE is built upon human-specific skeletal topologies, body models, and motion priors. Despite recent progress in humanoid 2D keypoint detection and HPE adaptation, humanoid-native 3D pose recovery remains insufficiently studied, and a dedicated benchmark with suitable training data and evaluation protocols is still lacking. To address this gap, we introduce Humanoids, a benchmark for monocular 3D humanoid robot pose estimation, and propose HumanoidPose, a framework for this task. Humanoids provides synthetic 3D supervision across diverse humanoid embodiments, manually annotated real-world 2D data, and real-world RGB sequences paired with robot states for 3D evaluation on a physical Roban humanoid. HumanoidPose combines human-inspired visual perception with robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. Experiments on Humanoids and the DHRP-H1 benchmark demonstrate strong performance in articulation recovery and 3D pose estimation, including zero-shot transfer to real-world 2D and 3D evaluation. Ablation studies further show the contribution of robot-native articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. The dataset and code will be publicly released to support future research in the community.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Clustering Algorithms in Targeted Preventive Care
abstract: In the modern healthcare, the importance of preventive care has came out as an effective approach in order to lighten the load of hospitals while also ensuring prolonged life span for patients. The current study on Clustering algorithms in targeted preventive care, highlights one such major issue in clustering algorithms that help uncover hidden patterns from a dataset to generate more precise preventative ac- tions in medical care. The core of this study involves a detailed comparative study of different clustering algorithms: K-Means, DBSCAN and Hierarchical Clustering. The methodology used in this study in- volves using various health datasets containing such features as age, body mass index, diabetes, asthma, arthritis, life style factors and geographical location, etc. The main evaluation factors to consider in regard to the algorithms include Silhouette scores metric, Scalability, Robustness and Interpretability. The results of this analysis, K-Means proves to be very efficient when dealing with huge, well-defined datasets. For this reason, it is suitable for population screening. However, when considering identification of outliers in patients having rare or unusual health problems, DBSCAN shows much better results. On the other hand, Hierarchical clustering gives much better insight into nesting various health risks. This report also focus on preprocessing, including scaling of data and handling incomplete values. Another interesting point of the analysis is that besides simple classification of health data, it may help predict chronic diseases, discovering some symptoms that would remain unnoticed during manual examination.

title: Learning Adaptive Defense Strategies: Fine-Tuned LLMs for Network Security Games under Network Mobility
abstract: Large language models(LLM) show promise for strategic reasoning, yet their ability to compute game-theoretic equilibria under dynamic conditions remains largely unexplored. This work investigates whether fine-tuned LLMs can serve as solver-free surrogates for online equilibrium computation in honeypot allocation, a setting in which network mobility continuously reshapes the underlying attack graph and forces repeated re-solving of a two-player zero-sum game. We construct a dataset of 270 security games on networks of 8--25 nodes with solver-grounded equilibrium labels, and evaluate four classes of predictor over 1{,}524 held-out mobility events: non-learned baselines, six open-weight architectures evaluated zero-shot, the same six after LoRA fine-tuning, and four proprietary models as an external reference point. Predictions are scored without post-hoc repair against exact game-theoretic criteria: exploitability against an optimal attacker best-response, equilibrium support accuracy, and distributional distance. Fine-tuning reduces exploitability across every architecture, and fine-tuned open-weight models of modest size outperform every zero-shot predictor, including proprietary ones; no zero-shot model at any tier reaches the floor set by uniform allocation. Stratifying by mobility type exposes a qualitative shift that aggregate metrics conceal: zero-shot models do not condition on whether a departing node lies on an attack path, while fine-tuned models recover this distinction. We further find that validation loss is negatively rank-correlated with task performance, and that output validity, rather than predictive accuracy, is the binding constraint on further progress.
